FROM MY DESK   Syracuse University has a $2.5 billion endowment, a storied 150-year tradition and a name recognized across the country. What it doesn’t have is enough of the students it wants. After scrambling last year to lure freshmen with additional merit-aid offers of up to $200,000, Syracuse fell short of its enrollment target this school year, sending it into a budget shortfall. Douglas Belkin and Roshan Fernandez trace how the problems that have long buffeted the nation’s smaller schools are now spreading to bigger, richer universities—with midsize private schools such as Syracuse especially feeling the pinch.

The Filipino tennis sensation knocked out three Grand Slam champions at last year’s Miami Open and arrives in New York ranked No. 18, the highest-ranked female Southeast Asian player in history. Now Eala faces one of the biggest tests of her young career in Flushing Meadows.

   • President Trump’s Venezuela deal caps months of secretive negotiations to give the U.S. rights to the some of the world’s largest proven oil reserves.

   • Icelanders voted against restarting negotiations on joining the European Union , the country’s national broadcaster said.

   • After issuing arrest warrants for Putin and Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu, the International Criminal Court has found itself caught in a geopolitical maelstrom that is threatening its survival .

   • Burger chain Steak ’n Shake has mounted an audacious turnaround strategy that embraces Trump’s brand of patriotism and the MAHA movement.

FROM THE MARKETS   • At Jackson Hole, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh quieted some concerns about his inflation-fighting strategy but set up a potentially bigger test three weeks from now : raise rates and risk infuriating Trump, or hold them steady and revive doubts about his willingness to act, writes Nick Timiraos.

   • Mark Walter’s insurers put billions into short-term loans to affiliated businesses, an unusual strategy that could ratchet up a funding squeeze on the Dodgers owner.

       4. READ IT HERE FIRST   A billionaire’s family feud has spilled into the boardroom.   Texas banking veteran Gerald J. Ford built his fortune buying distressed or undervalued banks and flipping them for big profits. Now, four of his adult children are suing to wrest away control of his more-than-26% stake in Hilltop Holdings, worth some $600 million. They allege their 82-year-old father is suffering from cognitive decline and being manipulated by his longtime second wife and others. Ford’s camp rejects that and says it is simple greed. Reporter Ben Glickman details how disagreements over estate planning morphed into a bitter succession drama that is now rankling the board of the company Ford forged.

   5.   Rich Americans have found another way to make their investments grow tax-free.   Think of it as a “Roth IRA on steroids”: The ultrawealthy are pouring billions of dollars into private-placement life insurance, a customizable insurance contract that allows unlimited investments to grow tax-free. They’re using the policies to invest in hedge funds, private credit and private real estate, alternative assets that can come with higher returns and hefty annual tax bills. But there is a major catch: To comply with Internal Revenue Service rules, investors have to give up control of the assets inside the policy. Miriam Gottfried explains how this once-quiet corner of life insurance has become increasingly popular.

The College Enrollment Crisis Is Coming for Bigger Schools
 
Plus, the 21-year-old Filipino tennis sensation making history, and the ‘Roth IRA on steroids’ attracting wealthy investors
 
 
MATHIAS SCHULZ/ZUMA PRESS
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Syracuse University has a $2.5 billion endowment, a storied 150-year tradition and a name recognized across the country. What it doesn’t have is enough of the students it wants. After scrambling last year to lure freshmen with additional merit-aid offers of up to $200,000, Syracuse fell short of its enrollment target this school year, sending it into a budget shortfall. Douglas Belkin and Roshan Fernandez trace how the problems that have long buffeted the nation’s smaller schools are now spreading to bigger, richer universities—with midsize private schools such as Syracuse especially feeling the pinch.

 

And as the U.S. Open gets under way today, keep an eye on 21-year-old Alex Eala. The Filipino tennis sensation knocked out three Grand Slam champions at last year’s Miami Open and arrives in New York ranked No. 18, the highest-ranked female Southeast Asian player in history. Now Eala faces one of the biggest tests of her young career in Flushing Meadows.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Russia has turned up the heat on Europe with a string of “gray zone” activities aimed at sowing fear. A meeting between leader Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping in Kyrgyzstan tomorrow will highlight their countries’ diverging fortunes.

 

• President Trump’s Venezuela deal caps months of secretive negotiations to give the U.S. rights to the some of the world’s largest proven oil reserves.

 

• Icelanders voted against restarting negotiations on joining the European Union, the country’s national broadcaster said.

 

• After issuing arrest warrants for Putin and Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu, the International Criminal Court has found itself caught in a geopolitical maelstrom that is threatening its survival.

 

• Burger chain Steak ’n Shake has mounted an audacious turnaround strategy that embraces Trump’s brand of patriotism and the MAHA movement.

 

• Watch: Famous financial adviser Suze Orman talks retirement, why eating out is a waste of money and why she doesn’t trust AI in our new video series My Monday Morning.

 
 
 

3. FROM THE MARKETS

 

• At Jackson Hole, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh quieted some concerns about his inflation-fighting strategy but set up a potentially bigger test three weeks from now: raise rates and risk infuriating Trump, or hold them steady and revive doubts about his willingness to act, writes Nick Timiraos.

 

• Mark Walter’s insurers put billions into short-term loans to affiliated businesses, an unusual strategy that could ratchet up a funding squeeze on the Dodgers owner.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

A billionaire’s family feud has spilled into the boardroom.

 

Texas banking veteran Gerald J. Ford built his fortune buying distressed or undervalued banks and flipping them for big profits. Now, four of his adult children are suing to wrest away control of his more-than-26% stake in Hilltop Holdings, worth some $600 million. They allege their 82-year-old father is suffering from cognitive decline and being manipulated by his longtime second wife and others. Ford’s camp rejects that and says it is simple greed. Reporter Ben Glickman details how disagreements over estate planning morphed into a bitter succession drama that is now rankling the board of the company Ford forged.

 

5.

 

Rich Americans have found another way to make their investments grow tax-free.

 

Think of it as a “Roth IRA on steroids”: The ultrawealthy are pouring billions of dollars into private-placement life insurance, a customizable insurance contract that allows unlimited investments to grow tax-free. They’re using the policies to invest in hedge funds, private credit and private real estate, alternative assets that can come with higher returns and hefty annual tax bills. But there is a major catch: To comply with Internal Revenue Service rules, investors have to give up control of the assets inside the policy. Miriam Gottfried explains how this once-quiet corner of life insurance has become increasingly popular.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

It’s getting crowded in low-Earth orbit.

 
 
MERRILL SHERMAN
 

There is more man-made material in space than ever before, raising concerns about collisions that could damage or destroy satellites. SpaceX’s Starlink satellites are already changing course more often to dodge potential hazards, and at least 41,000 more satellites are expected to be deployed to low-Earth orbit by 2034. We show you just how busy it’s getting up there.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING THIS WEEK

 

• Tuesday: Massachusetts holds primary elections. The Labor Department releases July job openings.

 

• Wednesday: Second-round play begins at the U.S. Open.

 

• Thursday: The Commerce Department reports the July U.S. trade balance.

 

• Friday: The Labor Department releases the August jobs report. Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh strike up an unlikely Cold War friendship in “Mayday,” arriving on Apple TV. Check out the rest of this week’s arts & culture agenda.

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
2032
 

That’s the year Social Security’s retirement trust fund is expected to run out of reserves. If Congress doesn’t act before then, benefits would automatically be cut by 22%. Lawmakers are trying to work up the nerve to solve it, but progress toward legislation remains slow and halting.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Job interviews now come with a new challenge: Prove you’re real.

 

Remove your Zoom background. Pan your camera around the room. Now, wave your hand in front of your face. As AI-assisted answering, deepfakes and fraudulent candidates complicate hiring, companies are upping their screening tactics to make sure job seekers really know what they’re talking about and are who they say they are.
